extracted.intended_audience: interested amateur and professional planetary observers / early-20th-century readers of planetary astronomy
extracted.subtask_description: Describing, measuring, classifying and interpreting the network of Martian 'canals' and associated spots (oases) from telescopic observations, including positional, morphological, seasonal and optical-detection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of doubles (double canals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The double is made by the addition of a second line in a particular position and not by a growth out to it of a line coincident to begin with with the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish true doubles (two distinct lines) from apparent duplications caused by atmospheric effects. Example contrast: Djihoun (always two lines when seen, lines keep same distance apart) versus Ganges (showed phases from swath to clarified double). Avoid attributing doubles to simple diplopia unless other evidence supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Width / separation measurement of doubles
rubrics_metrics.description: Average width between twin lines about 3° (degrees of latitude), with examples ranging from ~5°.1 (Ganges) to ~one-third of that (Djihoun); widths vary widely among canals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report widths in degrees (convert latitudinal degrees = 37 English statute miles). Do not assume a universal 'Martian unit' — widths appear to be individual characteristics conditioned by antecedent place and topography (examples: Phison and Euphrates widths predicted by foreshortening from their departure angles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Development / gemination and seasonal behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Canals exhibit phases: may appear first as a broad swath of shading, then clarify toward the center, and finally stand out as unmistakable doubles; show seasonal development with minima and maxima of visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document temporal sequence at each opposition; note ambiguous intervals where swarthy confusion precedes dual state (example: Ganges—clarification observed between months, minima in 1903). Do not conclude permanent bodily widening without sufficient repeated observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving power / limit of resolvability
rubrics_metrics.description: Some doubles (e.g., Djihoun) are 'very nearly at the limit of resolvability' — narrow features may be at the practical resolving limit of telescope + seeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether a feature lies near the resolving limit; recognize that small/close features may be perceived differently under varying seeing. Use repeated observations and improved sites/training to confirm borderline detections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shading versus distinct line distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Canals may appear as a confused swath of shading equal to or greater than later line widths before clarifying into distinct lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record transitional appearances (swath → clarification → double). Be cautious attributing widening vs clarifying: apparent widening may be due to broader shading that later resolves into two edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topographical conditioning of canal characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance between twin lines is an individual characteristic of the particular canal and in many cases conditioned by local topography (starting-points, bays, angles of departure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze geometric relations (origin points, foreshortening by angle to meridian) to explain widths and trends; use examples such as Phison/Euphrates and the twin bays of the Sabaeus Sinus to argue against a single engineered scale for widths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directional trend categorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize canal direction by compass sectors (eight compartments used here) to assess any preponderance of orientation (e.g., northeast-southwest vs northwest-southeast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Box the compass into sectors and tally canals per sector. Note that no conclusive preponderance may appear, but trends (e.g., a tilt east of north) can be discerned and related to hemispheric distribution and possible flow lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latitude distribution (zonal confinement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubles are practically confined to zones within forty degrees of the equator; 93% lie there, with none above 63° N or 35° S in the surveyed data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabulate occurrences by latitude bands (ten-degree zones recommended) and compare to area proportions. Use counts at particular oppositions and over multiple oppositions (tables A vs B) to show confinement and to argue that doubles are an equatorial feature rather than an observational projection effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitude distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Some meridians are more favored than others; example counts showed proportions roughly 2:5:3 among three 120° longitude bands (80°–200°, 200°–320°, 320°–80°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report longitude counts but consider whether longitudinal clustering is secondary to other (e.g., latitudinal or topographical) distributions before inferring significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with dark and light regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubles largely shun blue-green (dark) regions and polar zones; many doubles originate from or connect with the boundaries of dark regions (e.g., 28 of 53 proceed from the great diaphragm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map connections between light-region canals and dark-region canals; note whether canals contour dark patches or run from them. Use these associations to argue systemic continuity across surface types and to constrain origin hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity between light-region and dark-region canals
rubrics_metrics.description: Canals in the dark regions continue the lines of the light regions, linking the two into a single planet-wide system; dark-region lines were harder to detect but once seen matched and extended the light-region network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace where light-region canals leave the great girdle of seas and where dark-region canals begin; use repeated oppositions to verify continuity and to strengthen interpretation that the network is global.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarity / polar connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Canals continue into the polar zones, running at their northern ends into dark spots at the edge of the polar cap; polar snows thus appear to be connected to the canal system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document ends/terminations of canals at polar caps and note implications (e.g., polar origin or sink). Use these connections in arguments about system origin and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of spot (oasis) detection and appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Three stages: (1) scattering/wide dilution — invisible; (2) gray patch when atmospheric commotion lessens; (3) condensed black dot when conditions quiet and spot darkens and contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record time-resolved changes during an observing session to distinguish atmospheric smearing from true size/contrast changes. Recognize retinal summation contributes to line detectability whereas dots require good seeing to emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spot / 'oasis' classification by size
rubrics_metrics.description: Three kinds distinguished: large (about 75–100 miles diameter, ~2°; ~140 known), little (15–25 miles diameter), and a third 'less' category with collateral traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report measured diameters where possible and classify accordingly. Note that large spots are commonly the darkest markings, and that some small spots may have been sketched earlier but not recognized until superior observing conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical/retinal and atmospheric distortion cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retinal optics (tendency toward circular images) and atmospheric waves (condensation/rarefaction) can create illusions of shape, size, or duplication; faint lines may be visible by summation while dots of same diameter would be invisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly consider and report seeing conditions, scintillation, and possible retinal artifacts. Avoid over-interpreting shapes (e.g., apparent circularity may be retinal) and use multiple observers/sites to reduce such biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing true patches from spots
rubrics_metrics.description: True patches (groundwork of shading) differ from spots proper; patches can have superposed network of lines and spots but are distinct phenomena and should not be conflated with spots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate features that are extended shaded areas from compact dark spots: note tonal ground, extent, and superposed detail. Use comparisons with known examples (Trivium Charontis, Wedge of Casius, Mare Acidalium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and annotation conventions in cataloguing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use annotation symbols to indicate attributes (examples used: [*] wide canals, [+] northern hemisphere exclusively, [++] southern hemisphere exclusively) and separate counts by opposition (A = at single opposition; B = at all oppositions observed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt consistent annotation and tabulation (latitude bands, compass sectors, opposition-specific vs cumulative counts) to make catalogues comparable across observers and epochs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent doubles and transitional forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some canals (e.g., Arnon and Kison) are 'convergent doubles' that connect to polar caps and act as transitions between true doubles and true singles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and document transitional morphologies linking doubles and singles; such examples can indicate physical continuity and help interpret distributional sharpness (e.g., halting of dual condition near 40° latitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretative caution about engineered scales or cryptic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume canals widths or spacings reflect predetermined Martian units; examples (Phison/Euphrates, Sabaeus Sinus twins) argue widths arise from local geometry, not comprehensive design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer topographical/physical explanations supported by geometric analysis over speculative numerological schemes. Demonstrate agreement between predicted foreshortening and measured widths when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of measurement units and conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distances and widths expressed in degrees of latitude on Mars, with one degree of latitude equal to thirty-seven English statute miles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting distances convert degrees to miles for accessibility and ensure consistency in units across tables and descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal completeness and replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations from single oppositions may be ambiguous; repeated observations across multiple oppositions (and improved sites/training) are necessary to confirm developmental sequences and persistent features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate counts and statements by opposition (as done with columns A and B) and highlight which features are persistent vs intermittently observed; emphasize need for good seeing and repeated confirmation to reduce doubtfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global-network inference from connectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because canals continue from light regions into dark regions and to polar spots, the entire network is treated as a single planet-wide system with potential significance for origin/function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demonstrated continuities (maps/diagrams showing connections) as evidence that the phenomenon is later than and independent of the underlying background shading; avoid inferring purely geological background causes when network spans differing surface types.
